√वच् (adādi, 2P ‘to speak’), liṭ (perfect), prathama-puruṣa ekavacana, kartari prayoga

sandhi.note: The final s of ऋषिस् becomes ru. Not being at a pause or before an unvoiced sound, it does not become visarga (खरवसानयोर्विसर्जनीयः, 8.3.15, does not apply) and surfaces as r before the vowel: ऋषिरुवाच. After i (not a/ā) the r stays.

morph.note: Perfect of √वच् with samprasāraṇa in the reduplicated syllable (व → उ): उ-वाच. The standing formula of the speaker labels, as in 1.1.

mantras.anvaya_en: Subject and verb: a speaker label.

comm.t: Medhas, the seer of the frame story, takes up the narrative again for King Suratha (whom he will address as नृप and भूप in this chapter). Chapter 7 ended with Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa slain and Kālī named Cāmuṇḍā (7.27); chapter 8 tells of the Mothers and Raktabīja. In recitation this mantra carries the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the verse.

samasa.sense: Śumbha, named in the next verse

morph.note: Locative absolute (sati saptamī): a noun and a participle in the locative state the circumstance — चण्डे निहते ‘Caṇḍa having been slain’. The verse strings three of them (Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, the troops) before the subject appears.
Participle of a causative: पातय- ‘make fall’ + -इत. The same locative absolute, सिंहे च विनिपातिते, is in Śumbha’s order at 6.24.
From the causative of √क्षि (क्षययति ‘destroys’); the same participle described Dhūmralocana’s army at 6.20 (बलं च क्षयितं कृत्स्नम्).

mantras.anvaya: दैत्ये चण्डे निहते, मुण्डे च विनिपातिते, बहुलेषु सैन्येषु च क्षयितेषु, असुरेश्वरः (शुम्भः …)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three locative absolutes give the situation; the subject असुरेश्वरः waits for its verb, आदिदेश, in 8.3.
mantras.lit: When the Daitya Caṇḍa had been slain and Muṇḍa struck down, and the many troops destroyed, the lord of the asuras —
mantras.tr: When the demon Caṇḍa had been slain and Muṇḍa struck down, and their many troops destroyed, the lord of the asuras —
mantras.tr_note: The sentence runs on into 8.3, where the verb stands.

comm.t: A summary of chapter 7: Caṇḍa was beheaded (7.20), Muṇḍa felled (7.21), and their army was destroyed or fled (7.22). Each word for the deaths is a past participle; the defeat is stated as already complete.

The narrative pattern of the third carita is escalation: one general (Dhūmralocana, ch. 6), then two (Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, ch. 7), now the whole host. Each defeat draws out a greater manifestation of the Goddess.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (its member पराधीन is itself a tatpuruṣa: परस्य अधीनम्, ‘dependent on another’)
samasa.literal: one whose mind is dependent on anger
samasa.alt: The first two members may also be read कोपेन पराधीनम् (‘made dependent by anger’); the sense is the same: anger, not Śumbha, is in control.

samasa.vigraha: सर्वाणि च तानि सैन्यानि च, तेषाम्
samasa.sense: the whole army, not a detachment

morph.note: Perfect of आ + √दिश्: reduplication दि-देश with guṇa of the root vowel in the singular. With आ it means ‘command’; the object उद्योगम् is the thing commanded.
An s-stem bahuvrīhi (-चेतस्) lengthens its vowel in the masculine nominative singular: -चेताः (like सुमनाः).
The narrative particle ह, common in Purāṇic past tense, adds no lexical meaning and is usually left untranslated.

mantras.anvaya: ततः कोपपराधीनचेताः प्रतापवान् शुम्भः (असुरेश्वरः) सर्वसैन्यानां दैत्यानाम् उद्योगम् आदिदेश ह।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject of 8.2 (असुरेश्वरः) is now named: शुम्भः with two qualifiers; the verb आदिदेश governs उद्योगम्, with the double genitive saying whose mobilization.
mantras.lit: then Śumbha, the mighty, his mind dependent on anger, ordered the setting out of the Daityas, of all the troops.
mantras.tr: — Śumbha, the mighty, his mind wholly mastered by anger, ordered all the Daitya armies to march.

comm.t: Śumbha answers the loss of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa with a total mobilization. The narrator stresses that the order comes from a mind not its own master (पराधीन).

Through the Śumbha cycle the asura king acts from pride and anger (6.3 सक्रोधः, here कोपपराधीनचेताः), never from counsel; the tradition reads the asuras as passions that grow stronger the more they are opposed.
A modern reflection: the compound’s own word for Śumbha’s state is पराधीन, ‘dependent on another’. The mighty king is, in that moment, not free; anger has taken the throne.

षट् ‘six’ voices its final ṭ to ḍ before the vowel of अशीति.
The s of the prefix निस् becomes r before the voiced y.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (numeral compound of the śākapārthiva type, the middle word अधिका understood)
bahuvrīhi (prādi: the first member उद् stands for उद्यत)
samasa.alt: Some take Udāyudha as the name of a clan, parallel to the Kambus of the next line: ‘the eighty-six Udāyudhas’. The adjective reading is chosen because it needs no name the text nowhere else uses.

samasa.sense: each clan with its own troops

morph.note: Numerals from twenty upward are feminine singular nouns (विंशतिः, अशीतिः); they stand in apposition to what is counted or take it in the genitive. Both constructions are here: दैत्याः षडशीतिः, कम्बूनां चतुरशीतिः.
Third-person imperative (loṭ) of √या: a command to absent subjects, ‘let them march’.
Past participle of √वृ ‘to cover’, used for an escort: ‘surrounded by’ with the instrumental.

mantras.anvaya: अद्य उदायुधाः षडशीतिः दैत्याः सर्वबलैः (निर्यान्तु); कम्बूनां चतुरशीतिः स्वबलैः वृताः निर्यान्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Śumbha’s order in direct speech: two subjects, each a numeral, share the one imperative निर्यान्तु.
mantras.lit: Today let the Daityas, eighty-six, with weapons raised, (go forth) with all their forces; let eighty-four of the Kambus go forth, surrounded by their own forces.
mantras.tr: “Today let the eighty-six Daitya clans march out with all their forces, weapons raised, and the eighty-four clans of the Kambus, each surrounded by its own troops.
mantras.tr_note: What is counted is not named; ‘clans’ is supplied from कुलानि in 8.5. The plural वृताः is construed with the eighty-four by sense.

comm.t: Śumbha’s command begins (8.4–6). He names asura clans by number; the list conveys the size of the host rather than an order of battle.
The Kambus and the clans of 8.5–6 belong to the Purāṇic lore of the asura races; the text names them once and does not describe them again.

flags.uncertain: उदायुधाः may be an epithet (‘with weapons raised’) or a clan name (‘the Udāyudhas’), and the noun counted by षडशीतिः and चतुरशीतिः is not stated (clans, or chiefs). The translation follows the epithet reading and supplies ‘clans’ from 8.5.

samasa.sense: the Koṭivīryas, clans of immense might
samasa.alt: Taken by many as the name of a clan (Koṭivīrya) rather than a description; as a bahuvrīhi agreeing with कुलानि it serves as both: ‘the fifty Koṭivīrya clans’.

morph.note: A feminine t-stem numeral, used in the singular whatever the number counted: पञ्चाशत् … कुलानि ‘fifty clans’.
Vṛddhi taddhita (धूम्र → धौम्र) forming a patronymic or clan name: ‘those of Dhūmra’s line’.
Imperative third plural of निस् + √गम्, with the present stem गच्छ-; parallel to निर्यान्तु (8.4, 8.6).

mantras.anvaya: असुराणां कोटिवीर्याणि पञ्चाशत् कुलानि, धौम्राणां शतं कुलानि (च) मम आज्ञया वै निर्गच्छन्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two numbered subjects (पञ्चाशत् कुलानि, शतं कुलानि) share the imperative निर्गच्छन्तु; मम आज्ञया gives the authority.
mantras.lit: The fifty families of the asuras, of crore-fold valour, indeed — a hundred families of the Dhaumras — let them go out at my command.
mantras.tr: Let the fifty asura clans of the Koṭivīryas, and the hundred clans of the Dhaumras, march out at my command.
mantras.tr_note: ‘and’ is supplied between the two subjects.

comm.t: The muster continues: fifty Koṭivīrya clans and a hundred Dhaumra clans. The phrase मम आज्ञया makes the order personal; it returns in the next verse.

Dhaumra is formed from Dhūmra, ‘smoke-coloured’, the word that named Dhūmralocana (‘Smoke-eye’), slain by a mere हुंकार of Ambikā (6.13). Whether the text means his kin is not stated; the name may simply mark another asura line.
